subtopic: Handling a sudden job loss

Subject: could you look at my CV?

Dear Uma ma'am,
It's been two months since the layoff, and I've sent forty-two applications for junior data analyst roles. Three calls, no offers. Last weekend I finally stopped applying and looked at what I'd been sending.
I put my CV next to five job posts. Every post asked about results: 'reduced', 'improved', 'saved'. My CV only lists duties: 'prepared weekly reports', 'maintained dashboards'. Nothing says what changed because of my work, even though the churn report I built helped the team keep a big client.
So I've rewritten three lines with results. It's attached. Could you tell me honestly whether it reads better, and whether I'm aiming too narrowly? I've started looking at business analyst and operations roles too, since they use the same skills.
I don't want to keep doing the same thing and expecting a different answer.
Thank you,
Trisha

qa.a: Forty-two applications for junior data analyst roles.

qa.a: Trisha is frustrated after two months without offers, but determined to change the approach instead of repeating it.

qa.a: Ask former teammates what results they remember from the churn report, and tailor the CV for each adjacent role.

qa.q: How might Uma feel receiving this email?
qa.a: Likely pleased to be asked and impressed that Trisha studied the evidence first, which makes honest feedback easier to give.

Shankar, you asked what changed. Sit. I'm Amandeep, the one who applied to sixty design jobs and heard nothing, remember?
Two months of that. Then one night I stopped and made a table: every application, where it went, what happened. Sixty design roles. Four replies. All four said 'more experience needed'.
So I sent my CV to Professor Nair, from final year, and asked him to be brutal. He was. He said my CV read like a syllabus: courses, software, nothing I'd actually achieved. He circled the internship line and said, 'You cut the scrap rate on that line. Where does it say that?'
I rewrote it with the numbers. And I stopped applying only for design. Quality, maintenance planning, production support: they use the same drawings, the same thinking.
Last week, two interviews. Both in quality. It's not what I pictured, Shankar, but it's a start, and I know why it's working now.

The layoff call came at 5:40 on a Friday, and the HR manager, Vaibhav, said he had fifteen minutes before his next one. Trisha's hands were cold. She had a notebook open anyway.
'Before you go,' she said, 'can I ask four things?'
One: notice pay. Vaibhav said one month's salary in place of notice. She wrote it down. Two: pending dues, her unused leave and last month's incentive. He checked, and said both would come in the final settlement by the 15th. Three: health insurance. It ended on her last day, but he'd send the form to continue it privately. Four: a reference letter stating her role and dates.
'Can you put all of that in an email today?' she asked.
He hesitated, then said yes. At 6:10 the email came. Trisha read it twice, compared it with her notebook, and replied to add the one line he'd left out: the incentive.

Sarika didn't ask anything on the day her team in the Lower Parel office was cut. She signed the attendance sheet and went home in a daze.
The next morning, over chai at her kitchen window, she wrote a list. Notice pay. Salary for the eight days already worked this month. The unused leave. Health insurance, because her mother was on the same policy. A reference letter.
She called Joseph from HR at eleven and went through it item by item. Notice pay: two weeks, he said. The eight days: yes. Leave encashment: twelve days, yes. Insurance: ended with the job, but he could extend it for thirty days while she arranged her own. Reference letter: he'd need her manager to sign.
After each answer she said, 'Okay, noting that,' and wrote it down. At the end she read the list back and asked for it in writing. Joseph laughed a little. 'You're more organised than we are.'
The email came at four.

subtopic: Handling a sudden job loss
subtype: Approach: side income to cover essential costs [Revision]
passage:
I'm Suraj, and Simran and I share a flat in Indore. After her layoff she spent the first month doing nothing but applying, twelve hours a day, and getting nothing back. By the end of it she was checking her bank balance every hour and talking about taking a call-centre job she'd have hated.
Then one evening she turned her laptop toward me and said, 'Rent is ₹9,000. I need that covered so I can stop panicking.' She'd found two things: tutoring maths online to school students in the evenings, and writing short product articles for a small website. Neither was much. Together, she thought, around ₹10,000.
She took both. Mornings for applications, evenings for tutoring, weekends for writing. I noticed she stopped checking the balance so often.
In the seventh week she turned down the call-centre offer. Two weeks later she got an analyst interview. I don't know how she felt inside, but she looked like she could breathe.

qa.q: How much is Simran's rent?
qa.a: Rent is ₹9,000.

qa.q: What does Simran checking her balance every hour suggest?
qa.a: She was anxious and close to panic, which was pushing her toward a job she would have hated.

qa.q: Which change helped Simran most, and why?
qa.a: Covering the rent with tutoring and writing; it eased the pressure so she could refuse a poor offer and keep searching.

qa.a: Suraj notices the balance-checking stop and sees her able to breathe, while admitting not knowing her inner feelings.

I'm Lokesh, Madhav's friend from school in Varanasi, and I watched him plan the Pune move on my terrace, three weeks before he left.
He had ₹25,000 and a joining date. He drew three boxes on a sheet: BED, FOOD, COMMUTE. 'If these three work, I survive the first month. Everything else can wait.'
For each box he wrote options. Bed: a PG near the office, ₹9,000 with meals, or a shared room farther out, ₹6,000 without. Food: PG meals, or a tiffin service at ₹3,000. Commute: walk, or a bus pass at ₹1,000. He added it both ways, talking to himself. The PG came to ₹9,000; the shared room with tiffin and bus came to ₹10,000.
'So PG. And ₹16,000 left for the deposit and whatever I've forgotten.'
Under each box he wrote what he still had to do: call the PG, ask the alumni group about deposits. I don't know if he was nervous. He looked it, a little. But he looked like he had a list.

qa.q: What three boxes did Madhav draw?
qa.a: BED, FOOD, COMMUTE.

qa.q: How did Madhav seem to feel planning the move?
qa.a: A little nervous, as Lokesh saw it, but steadier for having a clear list of what to do next.

qa.q: What else could Madhav check before choosing the PG?
qa.a: How big the deposit is and whether the meals are good enough, by asking the alumni group or visiting on arrival.

qa.q: How does the planning look to Lokesh?
qa.a: Lokesh watches a scary move shrink into three boxes and a to-do list, and notices Madhav's nerves without being sure of them.

Monday, Pune. Her first bus ride takes 35 minutes. After the first month's fee and a ₹2,500 deposit she has ₹14,000 left, and the list is pinned inside her cupboard, two lines already ticked.

Lalremsiami, you're moving to Hyderabad next month, right? Let me tell you what worked for me. I'm Yash, and last year I had exactly zero contacts there.
Step one, I searched my college alumni list for anyone living in Hyderabad. Found fourteen. Messaged all of them, short and polite: joining in July, any leads on shared flats? Six replied. One added me to a flat-sharing group for our college people.
Step two, from that group I shortlisted three flats. I didn't pay anything online. People kept telling me, 'Just send the deposit, rooms go fast.' I didn't.
Step three, I took the train two days early and visited two in person. The first had no water after 10 a.m. The second was clean, ₹7,500 a month, and the senior living there worked in the building next to mine.
I paid the deposit there, standing in the kitchen. No broker. And a senior who showed me the bus route on day one.

qa.q: How many alumni did Yash find living in Hyderabad?
qa.a: Found fourteen.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt when people said 'rooms go fast'?
qa.a: Pressured and a little anxious, but determined not to pay a deposit for a flat never seen.

qa.q: What else could Lalremsiami do alongside these steps?
qa.a: Ask alumni what rent is fair in each area, so it is clear whether a flat's price makes sense before visiting.

qa.q: What might the senior in the second flat have thought of Yash's visit?
qa.a: The senior likely appreciated a newcomer who came in person and asked questions, which made sharing feel safer too.

grounding: Shows a newcomer messaging alumni, joining a college flat-sharing group and visiting two flats in person before paying a deposit.

I'm Preeti. I shared Ira's final-year hostel room, so I watched her plan the Bengaluru move from the bunk above.
She didn't just scroll rental sites. First she messaged the alumni coordinator for names of seniors living in Bengaluru. Then she joined a chat group of ex-students from our hostel and posted: joining in June, looking for a shared flat near Koramangala.
Within a week, two seniors had rooms. One sent a video; the other only photos. A broker had also called her, offering 'a great flat, pay the deposit today to hold it'. She said no.
In May she took an overnight bus and saw both flats in one day. She messaged me from the second: 'Video one smells of damp. This one's fine. ₹8,000, and the senior's nice.' She paid the deposit only after reading the rent agreement.
I can't say if she was scared. She sounded calm on the phone. But she didn't pay anyone she hadn't met.

qa.q: How much was the second flat?
qa.a: ₹8,000, and the senior's nice.

qa.a: She seems cautious and calm, unwilling to be rushed into paying for a flat she hasn't seen.

qa.a: The notice period, how the deposit is returned and what the rent includes, asking an elder or the senior to explain any unclear line.

'Rent's ₹6,500, and it's got a balcony,' Suraj said, holding up the listing at the tea shop. 'I'm taking it.'
Thomas, who had lived in Bengaluru for three years, sipped his tea. 'Walk me through a Tuesday.'
'A Tuesday?'
'From the moment you wake up.'
'Okay. Office at nine. The flat's in Hoskote. So bus to the metro, metro to Whitefield, then walk. Maybe an hour?'
'Maybe?'
'Say I leave at seven-thirty. Coming back, leave office at seven, home by eight-thirty, if the bus comes.'
'And if it rains?'
Suraj was quiet. 'Then I don't know.'
'So find out. Go tomorrow at seven-thirty and actually do it.'
The next evening Suraj called. 'Two hours ten minutes. The bus only came every forty minutes. Coming back was worse.'
'Still want the balcony?'

I'm Indu. When I moved to Mumbai for my first job, the cheapest room I found was with a retired teacher, Usha aunty, in Virar. ₹5,000 a month, home food, very kind. I nearly said yes on the phone.
Then I lay in bed and walked through a whole Monday in my head. Office in Lower Parel at 9:30. The Virar local, then a change. Wake at five-thirty, leave at six-forty. Coming home, the seven o'clock trains are the worst. Home at maybe 9:30. Eat, sleep, repeat. Where was the time for anything else?
Still, it was only imagination, so I tested it. The Monday before I joined, I did the journey at rush hour. I couldn't even get into the first train. It took two hours and ten minutes one way.
I called Usha aunty and thanked her. I took a shared room in Dadar for ₹9,000 instead. More money, but three extra hours every day.

qa.a: The extra ₹4,000 a month against the budget, and whether a middle option closer than Virar exists.

Placement office note, 20 June. Parul, placement officer.
Tarun came in before leaving for his first job in Kolkata, mainly to collect his documents. While I signed them, he told me how he had set up his move, and I'm noting it because I'd like to share it with next year's batch.
He opened a second bank account and put ₹13,500 in it: ₹1,500 for a sleeper-class ticket home to Ranchi, and ₹12,000 for one month's rent. He doesn't carry that account's card. 'It's not for spending,' he said. 'It's so I'm never stuck.'
Then he told his parents exactly what it was for, so that if he ever called and said 'I'm using the ticket money', they would know it was serious and not ask questions first.
He seemed relaxed for someone moving alone to a city he had never seen. He said the fallback was why.
I've asked him to email in a month about how the first weeks go.

qa.q: How much did Tarun put in the second account?
qa.a: ₹13,500 in the second account.

qa.q: Why did Tarun seem relaxed about moving alone?
qa.a: He felt calm and secure because the fallback money meant he could never be stranded.

qa.q: What else could Tarun add to the fallback?
qa.a: A written list of emergency contacts in Kolkata and at home, kept with the account details.

qa.q: How might Tarun's parents feel knowing about the separate account?
qa.a: Reassured that he has a way home, and trusted, since he told them exactly what such a call would mean.

Tomorrow night, the train to Bengaluru. First job, first time alone in a big city, and ₹30,000 total to my name.
Today I did the thing Lokesh dada made me promise. I opened the small steel box I got at Durga Puja and put in ₹11,000 in cash: ₹2,000 for a train ticket back to Howrah, ₹9,000 for one month's rent. Indu, write it down so you don't do it again.

I'm Ujjwal. In my first month in Noida I wrote down every rupee, mostly because my mother made me promise. On the 31st I added it up on the back of a delivery box.
Rent for my own room: ₹11,000. The gym I'd joined on day two because it was in the building: ₹2,500. Those two alone were almost half my ₹28,000 salary, and I'd been to the gym four times.
That was the moment. I knocked on Tanvir's door; he had the bigger room in our flat. 'What if we share your room and let mine to your colleague who's looking?' He thought about it overnight and said yes. The landlord agreed, and my share dropped to ₹7,500.
The gym I cancelled the same week. I run in the park now, which is free and honestly nicer.
In month two I finished with ₹4,000 saved instead of borrowing from my mother. It's not glamorous. But I'm staying.

qa.q: How much was the gym?
qa.a: The gym: ₹2,500.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel on adding up the first month?
qa.a: Ujjwal was startled and a bit embarrassed to see rent and a barely used gym taking almost half the salary.

qa.q: What else could Ujjwal track in month two?
qa.a: Food and travel, to see whether another category is creeping up, and keep the monthly tally going.

qa.q: What might sharing the room mean for Tanvir?
qa.a: Tanvir gives up some privacy but likely pays less too, which is why he thinks it over before agreeing.

grounding: Shows a newcomer tracking the first month, seeing rent and a gym take too much, sharing a room and dropping the membership.

Onboarding buddy note, day 45. Vishal, finance team.
At our first check-in, Ritu mentioned she was 'running out early'. I suggested she note every expense for the rest of the month. Today she brought the list.
She had highlighted two lines herself. Her single room in a shared flat: ₹12,000. A gym membership at the tech park: ₹3,000 a month, taken in week one, used five times. Her take-home is ₹30,000, so those two were half of it.
She told me what she had already done. She asked her flatmate, Deepa, whether they could share the larger room and let the small one go to a new tenant; the landlord agreed, and her rent drops to ₹8,000 from next month. She has cancelled the gym and joined the free yoga session the company runs on Wednesdays.
She said, 'I thought the city was just expensive. It was mostly two choices.' I'll check in again at day 90.

qa.q: How many times did Ritu use the gym?
qa.a: Used five times.

qa.q: What does 'It was mostly two choices' suggest about how Ritu feels?
qa.a: She seems relieved and more in control, seeing the problem was fixable rather than the whole city.

qa.q: What else could Ritu keep doing after these changes?
qa.a: Keep tracking for another month to check the new rent and the yoga plan hold, and spot any other leaks early.

qa.q: How does the change look to Vishal, who wrote the note?
qa.a: Vishal sees a small suggestion turn into Ritu's own decisions, and plans a day-90 check-in to support them.

grounding: Shows a newcomer tracking a month of spending, seeing rent and a gym take too much, sharing a room and dropping the membership.
